statement.p: Consider the vector field \vec{F} shown in the figure below together with the paths C_1, C_2, and C_3.

image.shortdescription: A horizontal vector field with three linear segment paths

description.p: Graph of a constant vector field pointing horizontally to the right. Curve C1 is a vertical line extending from a point to the right side of the graph upwards 1.5 units. The vector field points with constant length horizontally to the left Curve C2 is a horizontal line segment with a length 1.5, extending along the bottom of the graph from right to left. The vector field points with constant length horizontally to the left Curve C3 is a diagonal line with a length 1.67 extending from the top center of the graph down to the left, moving down about 1.5 units and to the left 0.75 units. The vector field points with constant length horizontally to the left

p.em: (Note: For the vector field, vectors are shown with a dot at the tail of the vector.)

statement.p: Arrange the line integrals \int_{C_1} \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{r}, \int_{C_2} \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{r} and \int_{C_3} \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{r} in ascending order:

?
integral on C1
integral on C2
integral on C3 \lt
?
integral on C1
integral on C2
integral on C3 \lt
?
integral on C1
integral on C2
integral on C3 .

static.solution:
\int_{C_1}\vec F\cdot d\vec r = 0, because the curve moves straight up and down, and the vector field points from right to left.
By similar logic, we note that both of \int_{C2}\vec F\cdot d\vec r and \int_{C3}\vec F\cdot d\vec r are negative. However, because C_3 has a smaller component pointing in the opposite direction as the vector field, the integral on C_3 is larger than that on C_2.
Applying this logic to each of the curves, we find that \int_{C_{2}}\vec F\cdot\vec r \lt \int_{C_{3}}\vec F\cdot\vec r \lt \int_{C_{1}}\vec F\cdot\vec r.
